title: Epidural in labor
what: An anesthetist places a thin tube in your back near the spinal cord. Medicine flows through it, and contraction pain becomes much weaker.
why: When contractions are very painful and you want pain relief. Sometimes the doctor advises it for medical reasons.
duration: placing it usually takes 10 to 20 minutes; it starts working in 10 to 20 minutes and lasts until the end of labor
tell_doctor: Blood thinners, and when you took the last dose
Allergy to painkillers or numbing medicine

prepare.title: In advance
prepare.text: Talk about pain relief with your doctor before labor. You can say you would like an epidural.

prepare.title: Tests
prepare.text: A recent blood test for clotting and platelets is usually needed.

prepare.title: Your decision
prepare.text: The anesthetist will explain the benefits and risks. You sign a consent form.

steps: An IV line and drip are placed
You sit and lean forward, arching your back, or lie on your side
The skin on your back is cleaned and numbed
The anesthetist inserts a needle and threads a thin tube, then the needle is removed
It is important to keep still. Say when a contraction starts, and the doctor will wait
The tube is taped in place, and the medicine is given
The midwife watches your blood pressure and your baby's heartbeat
feel: The numbing shot in the skin stings
Pressure in your back while it is placed
Your legs feel heavy, warm, and numb
Contractions feel like pressure, not strong pain
after: The tube comes out after the birth. It does not hurt
Feeling in your legs returns within a few hours
Get up the first time only with help from staff
Mild back soreness at the needle site can happen and passes
red_flags: A severe headache that gets worse when sitting or standing: tell your doctor right away
Numbness or weakness in the legs that does not go away: tell your doctor right away
Fever, pain, and redness at the needle site

faq.q: Is an epidural harmful to my baby?
faq.a: Usually not. Very little medicine reaches your baby. The midwife watches their heartbeat.

faq.q: Will I be able to push?
faq.a: Usually yes. Contractions feel like pressure, and the midwife will tell you when to push.

faq.q: Can I have it at any time?
faq.a: Usually in active labor. Sometimes it is too late or not advised. The anesthetist will decide.

reminders.text: Talk with your doctor about labor pain relief in advance. Keep your pregnancy record and test results in your hospital bag.
